column3: Flink has a switch to skip the stream alignment during a checkpoint (`flink-stateful-stream-processing#exactly-once-vs-at-least-once`).

column5: On a restore, these records will occur as duplicates, because they are both included in the state snapshot of checkpoint n, and will be replayed as part of the data after checkpoint n.

column3: A savepoint is a consistent image of the execution state of a streaming job, created via Flink's checkpointing mechanism (`flink-savepoints#what-is-a-savepoint`).
column5: A Savepoint is a consistent image of the execution state of a streaming job, created via Flink’s checkpointing mechanism.

column3: Savepoints can be used to stop-and-resume, fork, or update Flink jobs (`flink-savepoints#what-is-a-savepoint`).
column5: You can use Savepoints to stop-and-resume, fork, or update your Flink jobs.

column3: Savepoints differ from checkpoints the way backups differ from recovery logs in traditional database systems (`flink-checkpoints-vs-savepoints#overview`).
column5: Conceptually, Flink’s savepoints are different from checkpoints in a way that’s analogous to how backups are different from recovery logs in traditional database systems.

column3: A checkpoint serves as a recovery mechanism for unexpected job failures, while a savepoint serves planned, manual operations (`flink-checkpoints-vs-savepoints#overview`).
column5: The primary purpose of checkpoints is to provide a recovery mechanism in case of unexpected job failures. The use case for savepoints is for planned, manual operations.

column3: A checkpoint is created, owned and released by Flink, while a savepoint is created, owned and deleted solely by the user (`flink-checkpoints-vs-savepoints#overview`).
column5: A checkpoint’s lifecycle is managed by Flink, i.e. a checkpoint is created, owned, and released by Flink - without user interaction. Savepoints are created, owned and deleted solely by the user.

column3: Checkpoints are automatically deleted when the user terminates the application unless configured to be retained, while Flink does not delete savepoints after job termination or restore (`flink-checkpoints-vs-savepoints#overview`).
column5: Checkpoints are automatically deleted if the application is terminated by the user (except if checkpoints are explicitly configured to be retained). That means, Flink does not delete savepoints neither after job termination nor after restore.

column3: A back pressure warning for a task means it is producing data faster than the downstream operators can consume (`flink-back-pressure#back-pressure`).
column5: If you see a back pressure warning (e.g. High) for a task, this means that it is producing data faster than the downstream operators can consume.

column3: Back pressure is propagated in the opposite direction of the records, up the stream (`flink-back-pressure#back-pressure`).
column5: Records in your job flow downstream (e.g. from sources to sinks) and back pressure is propagated in the opposite direction, up the stream.

column3: The back pressure status HIGH means a subtask is back pressured more than 50% and up to 100% of the time (`flink-back-pressure#back-pressure-status`).
